strengths: Introduces ForeSeaQA, a new benchmark for surveillance video QA with image+text multimodal queries and timestamped temporal grounding across six subtasks, addressing an underexplored and practically important setting.

Proposes a practical plug-and-play VideoRAG pipeline that combines person tracking, multimodal embedding retrieval, and a VideoLLM; it is simple, uses off-the-shelf components, and achieves low end-to-end latency (2.6s) with a reduced frame budget.

Provides a broad experimental comparison against Video LMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, including ablations on spatial grounding methods and top-K retrieval, as well as generalization results on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.

The paper is generally clear, includes detailed data-generation prompts and implementation choices, and offers qualitative and per-subtask analyses that help expose remaining challenges such as counting and temporal localization.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: the system mainly combines existing components (ByteTrack, VISTA/GCL multimodal encoder, VideoLLaMA3) with modest prompt/metadata modifications rather than introducing a new retrieval or reasoning mechanism.

The main accuracy and temporal IoU gains are modest against the strongest VideoLLM baseline: average accuracy improves from 64.6 to 66.0 and IoU from 13.2 to 13.6. The abstract's reported 3.5% accuracy gain is relative to VideoRAG, not the strongest baseline, and absolute temporal IoU remains low (13.6), so the claim that ForeSea excels at temporal grounding is only partially supported.

The benchmark is relatively small (1,041 questions) and built from UCF-Crime, a single-camera anomaly dataset. This limits evidence for the paper's broader multi-camera and long-term surveillance claims. The benchmark lacks reported train/dev/test splits, inter-annotator agreement, annotation quality analysis, and data/code availability details.

Evaluation details are insufficient for reproducibility: it is unclear how native Video LMMs are prompted to output temporal intervals, whether retrieval-augmented baselines receive comparable frame budgets, and how negative search questions and temporal IoU conventions are handled consistently across methods.

The paper overstates 'first' claims without sufficiently discussing closely related multimodal-query temporal localization benchmarks and methods; multi-camera surveillance is claimed in the introduction but not actually evaluated.
There is no explicit limitations section or discussion of societal/dual-use risks for surveillance, privacy, and potential misuse, which would be important for a forensic-search system.

strengths: Targets an important practical problem: multimodal, temporally grounded forensic search over surveillance video, where text-only retrieval is indeed limiting.

Introduces ForeSeaQA, a new surveillance-domain benchmark with six subtasks, person-specific multimodal queries, timestamped annotations, and a semi-automated generation pipeline with prompt templates provided.

The ForeSea pipeline is modular and easy to understand: tracking, multimodal embedding, top-K retrieval, and VideoLLM reasoning. Using person-centric retrieval as an inductive bias is a reasonable system design.

Includes evaluations against several Video LMMs and RAG baselines, plus ablations on spatial grounding signals, retrieval depth, and retrieval backbone. The efficiency comparison suggests retrieval can reduce frame budgets.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ForeSea is primarily an integration of off-the-shelf components (ByteTrack/YOLO, VISTA/GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3). No new algorithm, training method, or multimodal embedding is proposed, so the algorithmic contribution is thin.

The benchmark is small (1,041 questions) and built solely from UCF-Crime, which is single-camera, often short-form, and not representative of the claimed multi-camera, hours/days-long surveillance setting. The abstract/introduction claims multi-camera and long-horizon video, but no multi-camera or long-duration evaluation is provided.

Benchmark construction relies on LLM processing of dense captions rather than direct video annotation. This risks language bias and dataset artifacts: questions may be answerable from captions without visual evidence. There is no control experiment showing that video is necessary, and no text-only caption baseline.

Manual verification is claimed but insufficiently documented: no annotator count, agreement, adjudication protocol, or quality-control statistics are reported. There is no dataset split description, release plan, license, or reproducibility statement.

The main ForeSeaQA average is not well-defined: text-only results average over six subtasks including counting and anomaly, while multimodal results average over only four person-specific subtasks. This makes the overall accuracy comparison across query conditions inconsistent.

The main results omit ForeSea-Global, even though the appendix shows it can outperform ForeSea (e.g., text-only accuracy 68.1 vs. 66.7 and IoU 18.6 vs. 13.3; multimodal IoU 16.1 vs. 13.8). This selective reporting weakens the claims of best overall performance.

Temporal localization remains very weak in absolute terms, with the best reported average IoU around 13.6–16.1. The metric for negative search examples (assigning IoU=1 when both ground truth and prediction are negative) may inflate averages and is not standard; per-positive-question localization should be reported.

Improvements over the strongest VideoLLM baseline are marginal and lack statistical support: ForeSea 66.0 Acc / 13.6 IoU vs. VideoLLaMA3 64.6 Acc / 13.2 IoU. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided for a benchmark of this size.

Open-domain generalization comparisons are not controlled: VideoMME and MLVU numbers are taken from original papers rather than rerun under identical prompts, frame budgets, and backbones. ForeSea mostly matches or trails VideoLLaMA3 on those benchmarks, so the generalization claim is overstated.

The latency analysis excludes offline database construction and indexing costs, which are critical for a surveillance search system. Hardware details and implementation settings are missing, making the efficiency comparison hard to verify.

Baseline adaptation is unclear, especially for multimodal queries. VideoRAG and T* were not designed for image+text surveillance queries, and their poor performance may reflect misconfiguration rather than true capability.

There is a methodological contradiction regarding cropping: the pipeline description says clips are cropped using tracked bounding boxes, while the default ForeSea ablation uses no Crop and only coordinate text injection. The role of cropping versus coordinate prompting is therefore unclear.

Presentation and clarity need substantial improvement: numerous typos and garbled notation appear (e.g., ForeSeaQA™, ForeSeaQA^RR, ForeSeaQA68/69, duplicated table text, inconsistent stage numbering). The meaning of ForeSeaQA^RR in the ablations is undefined.

The paper lacks a limitations section and any discussion of ethics, privacy, bias, or misuse risks. This is a serious omission for a surveillance and forensic-search system that could be deployed in sensitive real-world settings.

The method is person-centric, but forensic search often involves vehicles, objects, or global scene events. The approach and benchmark do not adequately address non-person targets, and this limitation is not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: multimodal forensic search in long surveillance video with temporally grounded answers.
Introduces ForeSeaQA, a useful benchmark with image+text queries, timestamped evidence, six subtasks, and joint evaluation of multiple-choice accuracy and temporal IoU.
The semi-automated data engine is reasonably transparent, with prompt templates and manual verification described, making the benchmark construction more reproducible than many prior efforts.

ForeSea is a simple, plug-and-play pipeline combining off-the-shelf tracking, multimodal embedding, retrieval, and a VideoLLM; the ablations convincingly show the value of person-centric retrieval and coordinate injection.
Reports both text-only and multimodal query settings and shows that ForeSea is more robust to the harder image+text condition than several strong VideoLLMs.
Efficiency results are promising: ForeSea reduces latency relative to prior retrieval-augmented baselines while improving accuracy on ForeSeaQA.
Generalization experiments on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench suggest the retrieval strategy is not solely benchmark-specific, which strengthens the practical relevance.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the system is largely an engineering composition of existing components (ByteTrack/YOLO, VISTA/GCL encoder, VideoLLaMA3) with no new learning objective or model architecture.
Benchmark scale and diversity are modest: 1,041 questions derived from UCF-Crime, with uncertain coverage of multi-camera scenarios despite the abstract emphasizing multi-camera video.
Multimodal query images are generated as crops from the same source video rather than independent reference images, which may simplify the forensic-search setting and reduce realism.
Manual verification details are insufficient: no inter-annotator agreement, annotator qualifications, verification protocol statistics, or explicit train/val/test splits are reported.

Temporal localization remains weak in absolute terms (around 13.6 IoU), and the average IoU improvement over the strongest VideoLLM baseline is small; multi-interval and negative-query IoU conventions are not fully specified.

Comparison fairness is not always clear: some baselines are taken from original papers while ForeSea is re-evaluated, and open-domain results use different frame budgets/prompts, so claims of matching or exceeding SOTA should be more cautious.
The paper lacks a limitations and societal-impact discussion, especially important for surveillance technology due to privacy, bias, and potential misuse concerns.
Strong claims such as 'first benchmark' and 'first VideoRAG system' may need more careful qualification given related work on multimodal queries and temporal grounding.

strengths: Introduces ForeSeaQA, a new surveillance-domain benchmark for video QA with multimodal image+text queries and timestamped evidence, covering search, activity, event, temporal, counting, and anomaly subtasks.
The semi-automated data engine combines entity extraction, visual grounding, grounded QA generation, and human verification, with prompt templates and metric definitions provided in the appendix.
ForeSea is a simple, plug-and-play VideoRAG pipeline using off-the-shelf person tracking, multimodal retrieval, and a VideoLMM, making the approach easy to reproduce and extend.
Extensive experiments compare many Video LMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, and include ablations on crop/overlay/coordinate injection, top-K retrieval, encoder choice, and VLM backbone.

ForeSea achieves the best overall accuracy and temporal IoU among evaluated methods on ForeSeaQA, with especially strong gains on search questions and lower inference latency than prior RAG baselines.
The paper provides useful open-domain generalization results on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, showing transferability beyond surveillance with a reduced frame budget.
The qualitative and sub-task analyses identify important failure modes, such as counting and precise temporal localization, which helps frame future work.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built only from UCF-Crime videos, which are low-resolution (320x240) and likely single-camera; despite the abstract mentioning multi-camera surveillance, no true multi-camera evaluation is provided.

Multimodal query images are crops taken from the same video/person entity, rather than external or cross-camera images; this makes the retrieval/re-identification setting easier and less realistic for forensic search.

QA generation relies on dense captions, and the oracle caption baseline reaches 83.2% multiple-choice accuracy, suggesting many questions may be answerable from textual descriptions rather than requiring fine-grained visual grounding.

Temporal localization remains weak in absolute terms: the best average IoU is only around 13.6% for the main ForeSea model, and even variant methods stay far from precise grounding, weakening the claim of precise temporal evidence.
The system is mostly a composition of off-the-shelf components (ByteTrack, GCL/VISTA encoder, VideoLLaMA3), so the algorithmic novelty over existing VideoRAG approaches is limited.
There is no clear statement that the benchmark, annotations, or code will be released, and there is little discussion of licensing, privacy, or ethical use for surveillance/crime footage.
Several tables and metrics are inconsistent or confusing (e.g., ForeSeaQA^RM/MM/HM naming, differing IoU values across tables), which hinders verification of the reported results.

Open-domain comparisons use an adapted frame-level retrieval pipeline rather than the person-centric method, and some baseline numbers are taken from original papers under potentially different protocols and frame budgets.
Manual verification lacks inter-annotator agreement statistics, and dataset splits/statistics are not fully described, limiting assessment of benchmark reliability and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets a real and underexplored problem: multimodal (image+text) queries with temporal grounding for surveillance video search, which is practically relevant and not well covered by existing benchmarks.

ForeSeaQA contains manually reviewed QA pairs across six subtasks, and the paper provides a semi-automated data engine with prompt templates and dataset statistics, which is useful for future work if released properly.
The ForeSea pipeline is simple, modular, and largely reproducible: it combines off-the-shelf tracking, multimodal retrieval, and a VideoLMM, and reports lower query latency than several baselines.

The experimental section covers multiple Video LMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, includes ablations on spatial grounding, top-K retrieval, encoder choice, VLM backbone, and attempts open-domain generalization.
The observation that person-centric retrieval improves search-type queries is plausible and could be a useful inductive bias for surveillance video understanding.
The paper correctly highlights that temporal localization and multimodal query handling remain weak in current Video LMMs and RAG pipelines.
weaknesses: The central claims are overbroad relative to the evidence. The title/abstract emphasize long, multi-camera surveillance and forensic search, but ForeSeaQA is built only from UCF-Crime footage and the method does not evaluate cross-camera person re-identification or multi-camera search. The multi-camera setting is asserted rather than experimentally demonstrated.

The benchmark may be substantially solvable from text captions. The oracle-caption baseline reaches 83.2% multiple-choice accuracy, far above all evaluated video models, suggesting that many QA pairs do not require visual or temporal video grounding. Since the QA generation engine is driven by dense UCA captions, the benchmark risks measuring caption understanding rather than forensic video understanding.

Temporal ground truth is potentially weak. Time ranges are assigned by an LLM from caption timestamps and then manually verified, but no inter-annotator agreement, timestamp precision analysis, or detailed annotation protocol is reported. The very low temporal IoUs overall further raise concerns about whether the temporal annotations are reliable enough for a grounding benchmark.

The evaluation does not actually enforce the claimed joint answer-and-localization task. Accuracy and temporal IoU are computed and averaged separately, with no joint metric requiring a correct answer accompanied by a sufficiently overlapping interval. The search-negative convention assigning IoU=1 to true negatives further inflates the temporal metric and mixes detection with localization.

The proposed method is mostly an off-the-shelf combination of ByteTrack, an existing multimodal retrieval encoder, and VideoLLaMA3. The paper does not introduce a new algorithm or substantial technical insight, and the core gain appears to come from a simple person-centric retrieval heuristic.

The main method variant is not the best-performing configuration. Appendix tables show ForeSea-Global and ForeSea-Hybrid often outperform the default ForeSea in accuracy, IoU, and/or latency, e.g., Table 3 reports higher overall MC/TL for ForeSea-Hybrid, and Table 4 shows ForeSea-Global with lower latency and higher IoU. The main tables and claims exclude or downplay these stronger variants, making the reported comparison feel cherry-picked.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently fair. T* and VideoRAG are adapted or reimplemented under different backbones, while the open-domain results compare ForeSea's own evaluation protocol against numbers copied from original papers with different frame budgets and settings. The paper does not provide a controlled same-protocol comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete. There is no clear statement that ForeSeaQA will be publicly released, no license/privacy discussion for surveillance data, no annotation code/evaluation code, and no details about how timestamped free-text outputs are parsed into intervals.

The retrieval backbone analysis contradicts the main encoder ablation. The appendix shows EVA-CLIP, SigLIP, and SigLIP2 often outperform the default GCL encoder, especially for multimodal queries, while the main text claims the encoder choice has similar overall performance. This weakens the justification for the default design.

Presentation and internal consistency are poor in places. Tables have garbled or inconsistent labels/columns, model names such as 'VideoLLaMA4-7B' and 'OCL' appear, and reported numbers differ across the main paper and appendix, making it difficult to verify the claims.

The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure modes of the tracking and retrieval stages. Tracking errors, missed detections, identity switches, and cross-camera identity association are critical for a surveillance search system but are not quantified, despite being central to the person-centric retrieval claim.

Ethical and societal implications of building a forensic search system for surveillance video are not discussed. Given the potential for privacy violations, bias, and misuse, this omission is notable for a surveillance-focused benchmark and system.

strengths: Introduces ForeSeaQA, a new surveillance-domain benchmark for multimodal image+text video QA with temporal grounding, six subtasks, and manual verification; this fills a real gap relative to existing long-video and surveillance benchmarks.

The ForeSea system is practical and well motivated: person-centric tracking drastically reduces the search space, multimodal retrieval supports text and image+text queries, and the retrieved clips are passed to a VideoLMM for grounded response generation.

Experiments are broad: main results, subtask details, ablations on spatial grounding, top-K, multimodal encoders, VLM backbones, caption-only baselines, efficiency, and generalization to open-domain long-video benchmarks.
The paper is generally clear, with implementation details, evaluation metrics, and data-generation prompts included in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
ForeSea shows consistent gains over retrieval-augmented baselines such as VideoRAG and T* on ForeSeaQA, and it is substantially more efficient in latency while maintaining competitive accuracy.
The multimodal query setting is important for forensic workflows, and the ablations suggest that person-centric retrieval is a useful inductive bias for identity-driven surveillance queries.
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively small (1,041 QA pairs) and constructed only from UCF-Crime, with low-resolution, largely single-camera footage. Despite the abstract’s emphasis on multi-camera surveillance, there is no multi-camera evaluation, and the system is not tested on cross-camera search or re-identification.

Query images are crops grounded from the same video/track used for retrieval and QA. This makes the multimodal query setting much easier than realistic forensic search, where a query image may come from a different camera, day, resolution, or domain. The benchmark therefore risks overestimating real-world performance.

The proposed method is mostly an integration of off-the-shelf components (tracking, multimodal encoder, VideoLMM), so its technical novelty is limited if judged as an algorithms contribution. The main contribution is better viewed as a benchmark/systems contribution.

By the authors’ own ablations, ForeSea-Global and ForeSea-Hybrid often achieve better temporal IoU and latency, yet the main table reports only ForeSea. The best-performing variant is not consistently used or evaluated in the main comparison, which weakens the central claim about ForeSea as the final system.

Temporal localization remains weak in absolute terms: even the best reported average IoU is around 13.6% in the main table (and still below 20% for variants), so claims about temporally grounded forensic search should be qualified.
The improvement over the no-retrieval VideoLLaMA3 baseline is modest (roughly 1–3 accuracy points and <1 IoU point on main ForeSeaQA), even though the improvement over weaker RAG baselines is larger.

Benchmark construction relies on dense captions, LLM-based QA generation, and manual review; there is limited information on inter-annotator agreement, annotation quality control, error rates, or dataset splits/release details. This raises concerns about annotation noise and caption bias.

Global tasks such as counting and anomaly detection remain challenging, and the person-centric retrieval design may not be optimal for them. The paper does not clearly describe query-type routing or adaptation for non-person-centric questions.
The paper lacks discussion of privacy, ethics, bias, and misuse risks for surveillance/forensic AI, which is especially important for this application domain.

There are several presentation inconsistencies and typos (e.g., VideoLLaMA4, OCL/GCL, HM/RM/MM notation) and missing main-paper coverage of LongVideoBench despite saying three open-domain benchmarks were evaluated.
